Plan by age · Stage 1 of 5

Ages 45–49: Peak years, full plate

For many households the late 40s bring the highest income so far and the highest bills at the same time: teenagers heading to college, parents who need more help, and a mortgage that is not finished.

Retirement is roughly 15 to 20 years away. That is long enough for savings to compound and for course corrections to work, and short enough that the next decade sets most of the outcome. This stage is about seeing where you stand and protecting the plan while the demands on your money peak.

Your first real retirement readiness check

What's happening

By the late 40s you have enough savings history to see the trend. A projection now tells you whether the current pace gets you to the life you want, while there is still time to change the pace, the date or the plan.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • How much of each raise or bonus goes to savings rather than spending.
  • Roth or traditional contributions, based on your tax bracket now versus the one you expect later.

Common mistakes

  • Treating savings benchmarks for your age as pass or fail. They are rough starting points that assume a specific income and retirement age.
  • Leaving Social Security out of the projection, or assuming it will be zero.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $24,500401(k), 403(b), 457 and TSP employee limit2026 elective deferral limit, before catch-up contributions.Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)
  • $7,500IRA contribution limit2026, traditional and Roth IRAs combined.Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)
  • $242,000–$252,000Roth IRA income phase-out2026, married filing jointly ($153,000–$168,000 single).Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)

Kids' college costs

What's happening

College bills often arrive in exactly the years when retirement saving is worth the most. Aid, credits and 529 rules can change what you actually pay, but each has its own forms and deadlines.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Pay from cash flow, from a 529, or with loans, and in what order.
  • Whether to take Parent PLUS loans, which are in your name, or keep borrowing to the student's own federal loans.

Common mistakes

  • Pausing or raiding retirement savings to pay tuition. Students can borrow for college; nobody lends you money for retirement.
  • Forgetting the education tax credit or double-counting the same expenses for both the credit and a tax-free 529 withdrawal.

Key numbers for 2026

  • up to $2,500American Opportunity Tax CreditPer eligible student per year, for the first four years of college. Income limits apply.Source: IRS: Education credits, AOTC and LLC
  • $35,000 lifetime529 to Roth IRA rolloverLeftover 529 money can move to the beneficiary's Roth IRA if the account has been open 15+ years, within annual IRA limits.Source: IRS Topic 313: Qualified tuition programs (529)

Caring for aging parents

What's happening

Many people in their late 40s and 50s start helping parents with money, appointments or day-to-day care. The cost shows up as cash, unpaid time off and travel, and it often arrives with little warning.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Paying for care versus providing it yourself, including the cost to your own career and savings.
  • Whether a parent who lives with you qualifies as a dependent or a qualifying person for tax benefits.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing a parent's money with yours, even with good intentions. It invites family disputes and legal trouble.
  • Quietly cutting your own retirement saving to fund care without a plan or a family conversation.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $7,500Dependent care assistance (FSA) limit2026, per household ($3,750 married filing separately). A parent can qualify if they cannot care for themselves and live with you more than half the year.Source: IRS Publication 15-B (2026): dependent care assistance

Protecting your income and family

What's happening

Your earning power is usually at its peak, so a disability or a death would hurt the household most right now. A few documents and policies protect everything else on this page.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Term life insurance sized to the years of need, versus permanent coverage.
  • How much of the emergency fund to hold in cash versus short-term bonds.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming workplace life insurance is enough; it often equals one or two years of salary and ends when the job ends.
  • Leaving an ex-spouse or a deceased relative as a beneficiary.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $250,000FDIC deposit insurancePer depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category.Source: FDIC: Deposit insurance

What's coming next

Ages 50–54: The catch-up years

At 50 the tax code lets you save more each year, and for many households the end of child-raising costs frees up cash at the same time. These are often the most powerful saving years of a career.

  • Catch-up contributions start at 50
  • Kids leaving home
  • Health costs jump
  • Divorce or widowhood in midlife
